title: Transatlantic Financing Corp. v. United States
summary: Closure of the Suez Canal did not make an available, more expensive Cape route commercially impracticable on this record, and the shipowner could not add the extra expense to its agreed price.
notes: Judge J. Skelly Wright's opinion (363 F.2d 312, D.C. Cir. 1966) states the three-part impracticability test: (1) something unexpected must have occurred, (2) the risk of that occurrence must not have been allocated by agreement or custom, and (3) the occurrence must have rendered performance commercially impracticable; the vessel was the SS Christos carrying wheat from a Gulf port to Bandar Shapur, Iran, and the shipowner sued in quantum meruit for the added Cape expense.

sections.Parties: Transatlantic operated the SS Christos. The United States chartered the vessel to carry wheat from a United States Gulf port to Iran.
sections.Material Facts:
The charter was executed during the developing Suez crisis. It specified the voyage’s endpoints but no route. The ship sailed from Galveston toward Suez; the canal was subsequently blocked. A Transatlantic representative requested instructions and extra compensation from a government employee whom Transatlantic conceded lacked contracting authority. The employee insisted on performance, disputed any entitlement to extra payment, and said a claim could be filed.

The ship went around the Cape of Good Hope and delivered the wheat. The cargo would not be damaged by the longer route, and ship and crew were fit to make it. The detour added roughly 3,000 miles to an expected 10,000-mile voyage. Transatlantic alleged $43,972 extra expense beyond a contract price of $305,842.92, collected the contract price, and sought the additional expense in restitution.
sections.Procedural History: The district court dismissed the shipowner’s claim. The D.C. Circuit affirmed.
sections.Issue: Did the unexpected closure excuse the original contract and entitle the shipowner to separate payment for completing the voyage by another route?
sections.Holding: No. The alternative performance was not commercially impracticable in the circumstances, and the proposed extra-payment theory was also inconsistent with treating the entire contract as displaced.
sections.Reasoning:
The opinion separates three inquiries: an unexpected contingency, absence of an allocation of its risk, and commercial impracticability. Suez was the expected route, but an expectation about the method was not itself a condition guaranteeing that route. Custom recognized the Cape as an alternative.

Foreseeability was relevant but did not conclusively allocate the closure risk. The court expressly declined to treat awareness of the political danger as a complete answer. It nevertheless considered the shipowner’s acceptance of abnormal risk when assessing the significance of the added expense. Suitable cargo, a fit vessel and crew, and the modest extent of the claimed increase defeated the impracticability claim.

The shipowner also sought to retain the contract’s profit while shifting only the unexpected costs to the government. If the contract truly no longer governed, a restitution claim would concern the value of the whole performance, not an automatic supplement for every extra expense. The court found no basis for preserving one side’s profit through that selective adjustment.

textbookImport.basis: Study paraphrase of the supplied tenth-edition casebook. No current-law/citator review.

learning.why: The case teaches the sequence for evaluating changed circumstances and the difference between predicting a risk, allocating it, and proving that it made performance impracticable.

topics.impracticability: Available alternative performance was not sufficiently burdensome to justify discharge.
topics.risk-allocation: An expected route and knowledge of danger did not conclusively assign the risk of closure.
topics.foreseeability: Foreseeability informs but does not replace the allocation and impracticability inquiries.
topics.restitution: A party cannot simply keep the contract price and demand all extra costs under an inconsistent restitution theory.
topics.ucc: The court uses Article 2 provisions as an analogy in a transaction not governed by Article 2.
topics.quantum-meruit: Transatlantic sued in quantum meruit for the added expense of the Cape route, and Wright J. rejected that theory because a party cannot keep the contract price and also recover the extra cost as if the contract were discharged.
topics.frustration: The three-part test (unexpected event, unallocated risk, impracticability) is the same framework courts apply to frustration-of-purpose claims arising from the Suez closure.

mnemonic.rationale: Around the Cape instead of Suez
